verdicts.note: KIDS COUNT child wellbeing indicators.
No abstract; 'Europe's demographic issues: fertility, household formation and replacement migration' names both links but settles nothing.
No abstract; an extension of the Brass relational Gompertz model is a methods paper.

Second demographic transition in Belgium and the Netherlands; its chapter 3 is 'The choice of living arrangement AFTER leaving the parental home', with fertility in chapter 4. Both links in one volume.
Journal issue table of contents; the grandmother-coresidency article it lists is screened separately.
Panel study of grandmother-grandchild co-residency among low-income families 1967-92. Prevalence and duration of the three-generation configuration; the arrangement is the outcome.
Living arrangements of single-mother families including co-residence with a grandparent, against CHILD DEVELOPMENT outcomes. The arrangement is the exposure but the outcome is the child's.
Untitled record with no abstract.

Cohort dynamics of the transition to adulthood across nine European countries, comparing median ages at LEAVING HOME, union formation, marriage and first birth. The whole chain, described rather than estimated, and the cross-national spread is the Wall 3 problem.
No abstract; leaving home, college, partnership and parenthood as predictors of LEISURE pattern stability. The outcome is leisure.
Trends in co-residence with children UNDER 15 as a measure of demographic parenthood. A different co-residence -- parent with young child.

IDENTIFIED LINK 1. Welfare benefit schedules that rise with family size as an incentive for teenagers to STAY in the recipient household, with the benefit rules as the source of variation. This is scope §4 design 6 realised, on the arrangement rather than on fertility -- the closest thing yet to exogenous variation in pre-launch co-residence. Priority read, and a candidate instrument.
French microsimulation of completed fertility; partnership behaviour is modelled, not estimated causally.
No abstract; embryo donation attitudes is decisive on subject.

Timing of family formation in Britain and Spain -- the high-leaving-late and low-leaving-late contrast that is the registered hypothesis's core comparison. Two-country design, so Wall 3's identification caution applies; full-text read.
Nineteenth-century female migration to Sundsvall.
Family and household in medieval England, with chapters on age at first marriage, family size, LEAVING HOME and servants. Pre-modern; A.7's under Ruling 2.

Leaving home across 16 European countries from FFS data, focusing on the TIMING, SEQUENCING and SYNCHRONISATION of leaving home with union formation. A gated anchor; the synchronisation measure is the closest published handle on §3's joint determination.
No abstract; men's flight from children, a historical essay.
Women's status and child morbidity in Kenya.
Area deprivation and teenage childbearing in Great Britain.
No abstract; 'Transition to Adulthood in Britain' is a country chapter in the European studies of population series.
Continuity of full-time employment among Japanese married women with an infant.
No abstract; encyclopedia entry on family theory in social demography.

THE aggregate statement of the registered hypothesis: across Western countries, the higher the share of 20-30 year olds living in the PARENTAL HOME, the lower the fertility, explained through familistic family structure. Cross-national association with no identification, so it documents the correlation the chapter must explain rather than an effect -- but it is the pre-launch arm's reference point.
Self-esteem and depression among Korean elders.
Asian population history volume.

Billari and Kohler's lowest-low fertility analysis, relating period and cohort fertility to LEAVING THE PARENTAL HOME, marriage and female labour force participation. Aggregate and descriptive, but it puts the exposure and the outcome in one framework across countries.
Childcare circumstances of Japanese nurses, first report.
Literature review of demographic change in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, whose stated general pattern is DELAYED TRANSITION TO ADULTHOOD and first birth. Southern Europe, descriptive.
Residence patterns of widows in preindustrial northern Europe.
Determinants of marital disruption in the Czech Republic.

Patrilineal and PATRILOCAL family system against Vietnam's fertility decline and the resulting rise in sonless couples. The arrangement is systemic rather than varying across households, so identification is the question; full-text read.
Children's economic roles among Maya subsistence agriculturists. C.3.a's.
Chinese caregiving burden for dependent parents and parents-in-law. The homonym.
Helicobacter pylori reinfection from a partner.
Psychosocial factors and health behaviours at menopause.

Living arrangements of 15-35 year olds in Europe and the US, identifying a Southern European pattern of extended stay in the parental home with DIRECT transitions from home to marriage and PARENTHOOD, against Northern and US patterns. The mechanism stated as a regional regime; cross-national, so Wall 3's caution binds, but it is the pre-launch arm's descriptive backbone.
Canadian men born 1916-1975: school completion, work start, HOME-LEAVING, cohabitation, marriage and FIRST BIRTH in one sequence analysis. The whole chain in one dataset, described.
Adolescent and young adult oncology.
First-time fathers' perceptions of preparedness.
Japanese co-residence as an asset for in-home elder care under population ageing. The homonym.

Argues Japan's falling birth rate is driven partly by LONGER YEARS OF CO-RESIDENCE with children who contribute little financially -- the parental side of the pre-launch arrangement, framed as a cost of children. Essayistic, but it states the mechanism from the parents' budget rather than the young adult's autonomy, which the scope's §1 does not.

Case studies of the Old Poor Law in England and LEAVING HOME in the United States 1850-60, as cross-sectional models. Pre-modern, but the Poor Law case is a policy-variation design on the arrangement worth reading for the design-6 enumeration.
Cuban-American elders increasingly living alone.
Induced abortion and perinatal mortality in Ukraine.
Living arrangements of elderly women in Lesotho.
Children's direct and non-direct effects on household demand.

Japanese nurses, rural versus urban: 68% nuclear households in the city against 60% living with parents-in-law and 20% with own parents in the rural group, with mean children 2.3 against 1.9 (p<0.001). A raw extended-couple to fertility contrast, uncontrolled and confounded with the rural-urban split (C.2.g), but it is a measured association in the extended arm.
No abstract; 'Families with Elderly: Are They Empty Nests' is decisive on the homonym.
Book review of a human population dynamics collection.
Feedback mechanisms in demographic microsimulation.
Review of demographic patterns in Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and the Baltics; companion to the Southern European review above.
Economic analysis of the family, textbook.
Women's education and labour force participation against fertility in twentieth-century Sweden. C.2.e's.
